FlashAttention sidesteps the memory bottleneck by fundamentally changing how the computation accesses data, rather than altering the mathematical result itself. In standard attention, calculating the $Q \times K^T$ product creates a massive $N \times N$ matrix that must live in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is slow and expensive to read/write repeatedly.

Instead, FlashAttention breaks the query, key, and value tensors into smaller tiles. It processes these tiles individually, keeping the active blocks in fast on-chip SRAM while streaming the rest of the data through HBM only when necessary. As each tile is processed, the partial results—specifically the running maximum and sum-exponential—are accumulated directly. This allows the algorithm to perform an online softmax update, combining partial results without ever storing the full attention score matrix in HBM.

The key insight is that while the total floating-point operations remain identical to standard attention, the memory traffic drops significantly, shifting the workload from being memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound.

Naive round-to-nearest quantization treats every weight independently using a single scale for a group, meaning an outlier in that group forces a larger step size that increases error for everyone else in that bin. AWQ flips this logic by observing that not all channels contribute equally to the output error.

Specifically, AWQ identifies which channels actually matter most by looking at their **activation magnitude** rather than their weight magnitude. Channels that see large activations during inference are the ones whose errors propagate most significantly through the network. Once identified, AWQ scales these salient channels down before quantizing them, effectively shrinking their dynamic range so the quantization noise has less impact.

This means AWQ attacks the problem by managing the range of critical data points instead of relying solely on rounding precision. It keeps all weights at low precision—avoiding the complexity of mixed-precision kernels—and relies on the preceding operation to absorb the scaling factor.

Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) work by rotating the query and key vectors in the embedding space by an angle that grows proportionally with their absolute position. As noted by Su et al., this means the attention score—which depends on the product of a query and a key—sees these absolute rotations cancel out, leaving only the difference in position [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)].

This creates a relative encoding scheme without needing learned position parameters or additive bias terms. Because the model learns interactions based on the *distance* between tokens rather than their fixed indices, it handles unseen sequence lengths more gracefully. When you pack multiple documents into one sequence, for example, the offsets cancel similarly, so the model maintains consistent relative distances without resetting position IDs [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)].

Think of it like measuring the gap between two people standing in a line; it doesn't matter where the line starts, only how many steps apart they are.
